```{python}
import json
import warnings
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.dates as mdates
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
from IPython.display import HTML

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=UserWarning)

POST_DIR = Path(".").resolve()
CLEAN_DIR = POST_DIR / "data" / "clean"
IMG_DIR = POST_DIR / "images"
STATS_DIR = POST_DIR / "stats"
IMG_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

with open(STATS_DIR / "summary_stats.json", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    stats = json.load(f)

# One palette. The Treasury yield stays blue. The listing bars reuse the same hues.
COLORS = {
    "primary": "#2e5984",
    "accent": "#8b0000",
    "secondary": "#6b8e6b",
    "neutral": "#4a4a4a",
    "light": "#b0b0b0",
    "warning": "#cc7722",
    "fed_target": "#cc0000",
}

plt.rcParams.update({
    "font.family": "Calibri",
    "font.size": 10,
    "axes.labelsize": 10,
    "axes.titlesize": 11,
    "xtick.labelsize": 9,
    "ytick.labelsize": 9,
    "legend.fontsize": 8,
    "axes.spines.top": False,
    "axes.spines.right": False,
    "axes.grid": False,
    "axes.linewidth": 0.5,
    "lines.linewidth": 1.8,
    "figure.facecolor": "white",
    "axes.facecolor": "#fafafa",
    "figure.dpi": 100,
})


def fmt(n, digits=1):
    """Format a level. Floats default to one decimal."""
    return f"{float(n):,.{digits}f}"


def fmt_chg(n, digits=1):
    """Format a signed change."""
    return f"{float(n):+,.{digits}f}"


def fmt2(n):
    """Two decimals for a yield or a reported share price."""
    return f"{float(n):.2f}"


def fmt_usd(n):
    """Dollar sign stays inside the expression so Markdown does not treat it as math."""
    return f"${float(n):,.2f}"


def short_year(label):
    """Print 2026 as 26. The stats file keeps the four-digit year."""
    return str(label).replace("2026", "26")


def month_tick(value, _pos=None):
    """Month ticks. Only 2026 is shortened."""
    stamp = mdates.num2date(value)
    year = "26" if stamp.year == 2026 else str(stamp.year)
    return f"{stamp.strftime('%b')}\n{year}"


def short_stamp(stamp):
    """US month/day from a timestamp. Only 2026 is shortened."""
    year = "26" if stamp.year == 2026 else str(stamp.year)
    return f"{stamp.month}/{stamp.day}/{year}"


for key, value in list(stats.items()):
    if isinstance(value, str):
        stats[key] = short_year(value)
```

The Fed's October meeting raised two distinct concerns about AI investment: pressure on prices today, and financing losses if future returns disappoint. Many participants discussed the AI buildout as a source of inflation pressure. The staff separately warned that leasing commitments and financing between related AI firms could magnify losses if the investments earned less than expected. These were conditional risks, not a finding that an AI bubble had burst. The [October meeting minutes](https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomcminutes20261028.htm) record both concerns.

The Committee met on `{python} stats['fomc_meeting_start']` and `{python} stats['fomc_decision_date']`. Its minutes became public on `{python} stats['minutes_date']`. Anthropic shares began public trading the next day, `{python} stats['ipo_open_date']`, following its initial public offering (IPO), its first sale of shares to public investors. This post puts that stock-market debut beside the Fed's discussion and the Treasury-yield backdrop. It does not treat the debut as proof of the Fed's concerns or as a reaction caused by the minutes. The minutes do not name Anthropic, and the [release notice](https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20261118a.htm) says they describe only information available at the October meeting.

The reported price sequence is simple. Investors allocated shares in the IPO paid `{python} fmt_usd(stats['ipo_offer'])` per share. The first public-market trade was at `{python} fmt_usd(stats['ipo_open'])`, and the stock ended that day at `{python} fmt_usd(stats['ipo_day1_close'])`. It ended the next trading day, `{python} stats['ipo_day2_date']`, at `{python} fmt_usd(stats['ipo_day2_close'])`. A "close" means the share price at the end of a trading day. It is not another share offering. The [price section below](#anthropics-first-two-trading-days) separates the dates and starting prices used in each comparison.

The target range for the federal funds rate, an overnight interest rate on loans between banks, stayed at `{python} fmt2(stats['funds_lower'])` to `{python} fmt2(stats['funds_upper'])`%. `{python} stats['vote_for_hold']` voting members favored leaving the rate unchanged; `{python} stats['vote_for_hike']` favored a quarter-percentage-point increase. The [October decision statement](https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20261028a.htm) records that vote. The participant counts above are the discussion. The vote counts are the members who set the range.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Reproducing this analysis

The Python code used to generate each chart is included in this post. Click on any code block to see the full implementation. The complete data pipeline includes:

- `01_fetch_data.py` checks the saved FRED vintages and does not download
- `02_clean_data.py` writes the cleaned yield file the chart plots
- `04_compute_stats.py` writes the figures quoted in the text, including the share-price comparisons

The 10-year yield uses the `{python} stats['yield_release_date']` H.15 vintage and ends on `{python} stats['dgs10_latest_date']`. The IPO and public-market prices are transcribed market reports, with source links beside the price comparison. The pipeline still checks the CPI, PPI, and PCE files behind the one-paragraph backdrop. The default command checks the saved files and does not download a new copy.

The inflation figures in the bridge are the same locked October prints as the November 14 post. This post does not fill the missing CPI year rate. The 10-year yield is an official series. The yield card is an annualized interest rate, not a daily investment return. The IPO price applies to investors allocated shares before public trading, not to everyone who later bought the stock. The day-two card measures the change from the `{python} stats['ipo_open_date']` closing price to the `{python} stats['ipo_day2_date']` closing price.

## The inflation prints are unchanged

[October prices rose, but the annual CPI comparison is missing](https://gilboa.blog/posts/2026-11-14-october-cpi-ppi-missing-annual/) already covered the October inflation prints. In `{python} stats['latest_month']`, consumer prices rose `{python} fmt(stats['cpi_mom'])`% and core prices rose `{python} fmt(stats['cpi_core_mom'])`%. There is still no official 12-month CPI rate, because `{python} stats['gap_month']` was not collected. Producer prices rose `{python} fmt(stats['ppi_yoy'])`% over the year. CPI was released `{python} stats['cpi_release_date']` and PPI `{python} stats['ppi_release_date']`, both after the decision on `{python} stats['fomc_decision_date']`. Those prints have not changed. They are background, not a new result.

## What the minutes say

### The policy judgment

Most participants supported holding the target range at this meeting. Many of them wanted more information before deciding the stance that would return inflation to the Committee's `{python} fmt(stats['fed_target'], 0)`% goal. The staff estimate in hand was that total PCE inflation was `{python} fmt(stats['pce_yoy'])`% in `{python} stats['pce_month']`. Most participants said inflation pressures were broad based. Many called the AI buildout a material source of inflation risk. Many also observed that demand for those products was straining supply and raising prices. Those comments are about prices. They are separate from the valuation scenario below, and the [October minutes](https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomcminutes20261028.htm) record them.

For the months ahead, almost all participants judged that further increases would likely be appropriate under baseline outlooks broadly consistent with the September projections. That projection's median funds rate at `{python} stats['sep_horizon']` was `{python} fmt(stats['sep_end_2026_median'])`% in the [September Summary of Economic Projections](https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomcprojtabl20260916.htm). A couple of participants said an increase of more than a quarter point could warrant consideration at the next meeting if the inflation data were unfavorable. Participants also said later decisions would depend on the incoming data, the outlook, and the balance of risks. The judgment is conditional. It is not a vote on the December meeting. The [October minutes](https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomcminutes20261028.htm) record that judgment.

### Financial-stability comments

The staff briefing used severe scenarios, not a forecast that those scenarios would occur. The staff highlighted how fast debt tied to the AI buildout had grown. Some of that financing is leasing that does not appear as an ordinary loan, and some of it runs between related AI firms. The staff's point was that those links could magnify losses if the investment returns disappointed. Elevated asset valuations and hedge-fund leverage were the vulnerabilities the staff called most salient. Stronger bank and household balance sheets were described as a buffer. The staff did not report that an AI bubble had been established. This paragraph follows the [staff assessment in the minutes](https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomcminutes20261028.htm).

In the discussion that followed, almost all participants commented on the disappointing-returns scenario, and many commented on an AI-related revaluation of asset prices should it occur. Most observed that AI-related debt had grown quickly, much of it through financing structures that are complex and hard to see through. Several participants said financial conditions were still supportive of growth, citing elevated equity valuations and widely available credit. A majority, though, noted tighter conditions since the September meeting, including wider credit spreads for some higher-risk and AI-related borrowers. Several stressed that monetary policy was not the right tool for addressing financial-stability risk directly. This paragraph follows the [participants' discussion in the minutes](https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomcminutes20261028.htm).

### What the manager reported about markets

The manager's account covers the period between Fed meetings, ending before `{python} stats['fomc_decision_date']`. It therefore predates Anthropic's stock-market debut. On net, the manager said nominal Treasury yields were little changed over that window, after a rise into early October on stronger data and a later pullback. In that account, the pullback came with uncertainty about AI firms' revenue and about the pace of data-center construction, and with concern over French government debt. Equity prices in the AI infrastructure segment rose earlier in the period. Risk sentiment then worsened after two leading AI firms reported revenue growth below what investors expected, and after a large cloud-computing company laid out spending plans that needed more financing than investors had anticipated. The minutes do not give those firms' names. The manager also said that a higher rate level had already been weighing on equity prices and raising credit spreads before this period. This paragraph follows the [market manager's account in the minutes](https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomcminutes20261028.htm).

## The yield backdrop

The official series in the `{python} stats['yield_release_date']` H.15 vintage ends on `{python} stats['dgs10_latest_date']`. The last observation is `{python} fmt(stats['dgs10_latest'], 2)`%. The vintage date and that observation date are not the same, and the file has no yield for `{python} stats['ipo_day2_date']`. The [live DGS10 series](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DGS10) may contain later observations or revisions. That page is the current series, not a frozen copy of the saved vintage. The high in this file is `{python} fmt(stats['dgs10_high_2026'], 2)`% on `{python} stats['dgs10_high_2026_date']`, before the meeting. The yield was `{python} fmt(stats['dgs10_meeting_day'], 2)`% on the decision date, `{python} fmt(stats['dgs10_week_ago'], 2)`% on `{python} stats['dgs10_week_ago_date']`, and `{python} fmt(stats['dgs10_minutes_day'], 2)`% when the minutes came out.

A nominal Treasury yield mixes expected short-term rates, compensation for inflation, and a term premium, the extra compensation investors require for holding a longer-term bond. This post does not split those parts. Higher required returns reduce what investors will pay today for cash flows expected far in the future. That makes rates relevant to growth stocks, but a Treasury yield is not the whole return investors require from a stock. This yield path does not establish why Anthropic's share price fell during its first two trading days.

The blue line is the 10-year Treasury yield. The labeled peak is the high in this window. The gray line marks the Fed's meeting decision, and the red line marks Anthropic's first public trading day. The minutes were released one day before that red line. At this chart's scale, a separate release-date line would sit almost on top of it. On a phone, swipe horizontally within the chart to see the full date range.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| label: fig-yield-backdrop
#| fig-cap: "The 10-year yield ended this H.15 vintage at 5.04 percent on November 19. Gray marks the Fed's decision; red marks Anthropic's first public trading day, one day after the minutes were released. These dates do not establish what caused the stock-price changes."
#| fig-alt: "Blue line of the 10-year yield from June 26 to November 19, 26. The peak is 5.31 percent on October 5 and the last point is 5.04 percent. A gray dashed line marks October 28 and a red dashed line marks November 19."

# Cleaned H.15 yields only. Holiday blanks stay off the line because the axis is a date.
yields = pd.read_csv(CLEAN_DIR / "yields_daily.csv", index_col="date", parse_dates=True)
yields = yields.loc["2026-06-01":].dropna(subset=["dgs10"])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.0, 4.8))
ax.plot(yields.index, yields["dgs10"], color=COLORS["primary"])

high_x = yields["dgs10"].idxmax()
high_y = float(yields.loc[high_x, "dgs10"])
last_x = yields.index.max()
last_y = float(yields.iloc[-1]["dgs10"])
for x_val, y_val in ((high_x, high_y), (last_x, last_y)):
    ax.scatter([x_val], [y_val], s=40, color=COLORS["primary"], edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.8, zorder=4)

ax.annotate(
    f"{high_y:.2f}%",
    xy=(high_x, high_y),
    xytext=(0, 8),
    textcoords="offset points",
    color=COLORS["primary"],
    fontsize=8,
    fontweight="bold",
    ha="center",
    va="bottom",
    annotation_clip=False,
    zorder=5,
)
ax.annotate(
    f"{last_y:.2f}%\n{short_stamp(last_x)}",
    xy=(last_x, last_y),
    xytext=(8, 0),
    textcoords="offset points",
    color=COLORS["primary"],
    fontsize=8,
    fontweight="bold",
    ha="left",
    va="center",
    annotation_clip=False,
    zorder=5,
)

meeting = pd.to_datetime(stats["fomc_decision_date"], format="%m/%d/%y")
listing = pd.to_datetime(stats["ipo_open_date"], format="%m/%d/%y")
ax.axvline(meeting, color=COLORS["neutral"], linewidth=1.0, linestyle="--", zorder=1)
ax.axvline(listing, color=COLORS["accent"], linewidth=1.0, linestyle="--", zorder=1)

ax.set_ylabel("10-year yield, percent")
ax.xaxis.set_major_locator(mdates.MonthLocator())
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(month_tick))
start, end = yields.index.min(), yields.index.max()
ax.set_xlim(start, end + (end - start) * 0.16)
y_min = float(yields["dgs10"].min())
y_max = float(yields["dgs10"].max())
pad = (y_max - y_min) * 0.16
ax.set_ylim(y_min - pad * 0.25, y_max + pad)
ax.text(
    0.02,
    0.98,
    (
        f"Gray line: meeting ended {stats['fomc_decision_date']}\n"
        f"Red line: Anthropic trading begins {stats['ipo_open_date']}\n"
        f"Minutes were {stats['minutes_date']}, one day earlier.\n"
        "Dates, not identified causes."
    ),
    transform=ax.transAxes,
    fontsize=8,
    color=COLORS["neutral"],
    ha="left",
    va="top",
    bbox={"boxstyle": "round,pad=0.25", "fc": "#fafafa", "ec": "none", "alpha": 0.92},
    zorder=5,
)
plt.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(IMG_DIR / "yield-backdrop.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
```

## Anthropic's first two trading days

The IPO price and the public-market prices answer different questions. The IPO price is what investors allocated shares paid before trading began. The first public trade is what a buyer paid when trading started. Each day's closing price is a later market observation, not another sale by the company.

| Stage | When | Reported price per share |
| --- | --- | --- |
| IPO allocation | Before public trading | `{python} fmt_usd(stats['ipo_offer'])` |
| First public trade | `{python} stats['ipo_open_date']`, trading begins | `{python} fmt_usd(stats['ipo_open'])` |
| Day-one close | `{python} stats['ipo_open_date']`, end of trading | `{python} fmt_usd(stats['ipo_day1_close'])` |
| Day-two close | `{python} stats['ipo_day2_date']`, end of trading | `{python} fmt_usd(stats['ipo_day2_close'])` |

: Anthropic's reported IPO price followed by three public-market observations, in chronological order.

By the end of day two, the stock was down `{python} fmt(abs(stats['ipo_day2_vs_day1_pct']))`% from the previous day's close and `{python} fmt(abs(stats['ipo_day2_vs_open_pct']))`% from its first public trade. It was still `{python} fmt(stats['ipo_day2_vs_offer_pct'])`% above the IPO price. Those statements are consistent: each uses a different starting price. An IPO investor and someone who bought the first public trade did not pay the same amount.

| Price comparison | Change | Starting price |
| --- | --- | --- |
| IPO price to first public trade | `{python} fmt_chg(stats['ipo_open_vs_offer_pct'])`% | `{python} fmt_usd(stats['ipo_offer'])` IPO price |
| First public trade to day-one close | `{python} fmt_chg(stats['ipo_day1_vs_open_pct'])`% | `{python} fmt_usd(stats['ipo_open'])` first public trade |
| Day-one close to day-two close | `{python} fmt_chg(stats['ipo_day2_vs_day1_pct'])`% | `{python} fmt_usd(stats['ipo_day1_close'])` day-one close |
| First public trade to day-two close | `{python} fmt_chg(stats['ipo_day2_vs_open_pct'])`% | `{python} fmt_usd(stats['ipo_open'])` first public trade |
| IPO price to day-two close | `{python} fmt_chg(stats['ipo_day2_vs_offer_pct'])`% | `{python} fmt_usd(stats['ipo_offer'])` IPO price |

: Each percentage compares the ending price with the starting price in its row. A positive change from the IPO price can coexist with a decline after public trading begins.

The [Forbes report on the first trading day](https://www.forbes.com/sites/fionariley/2026/11/19/anthropic-ipo-live-stock-closes-day-at-97-up-more-than-17/) is the saved source attribution for the IPO price, first public trade, and day-one close. The [Motley Fool page on the second trading day](https://www.fool.com/investing/2026/11/20/why-anthropic-stock-is-falling-today/) shows the day-two price with the quote label "As of 4:00 PM ET" and the date `{python} stats['ipo_day2_date']`. Its article text describes an earlier, 11:15 a.m. observation, which is not the closing price used here. Neither page is archived with this post, and the original transcription has no retrieval timestamp.

The chart follows the same sequence as the first table. Gray is the IPO price, red is the first public trade, blue is the day-one close, and orange is the day-two close. On a phone, swipe horizontally within the chart to see all four prices.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| label: fig-listing-prices
#| fig-cap: "Anthropic's day-two closing price remained above its IPO price but below its first public trade and day-one close. The gray bar is the price paid in the IPO; the other bars are public-market observations."
#| fig-alt: "Anthropic prices in chronological order: IPO price 83 dollars before trading; first public trade 111.50 and day-one close 97.17 on November 19, 26; day-two close 88.91 on November 20, 26."

prices = pd.Series(
    {
        "IPO price": stats["ipo_offer"],
        "First public trade": stats["ipo_open"],
        "Day-one close": stats["ipo_day1_close"],
        "Day-two close": stats["ipo_day2_close"],
    }
)
tick_labels = [
    "IPO price\nBefore trading",
    f"First public trade\n{stats['ipo_open_date']}",
    f"Day-one close\n{stats['ipo_open_date']}",
    f"Day-two close\n{stats['ipo_day2_date']}",
]
bar_colors = [COLORS["neutral"], COLORS["accent"], COLORS["primary"], COLORS["warning"]]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.0, 4.5))
positions = list(range(len(prices)))
ax.bar(positions, prices.values, color=bar_colors, width=0.72)
span = float(prices.max() - prices.min())
pad = span * 0.08
for pos, value in zip(positions, prices.values):
    ax.text(
        pos,
        value + pad,
        f"{value:,.2f}",
        ha="center",
        va="bottom",
        fontsize=8,
        color=COLORS["neutral"],
    )
ax.set_xticks(positions)
ax.set_xticklabels(tick_labels)
ax.set_ylabel("Reported share price, dollars")
ax.set_ylim(0, float(prices.max()) + pad * 4)
plt.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(IMG_DIR / "listing-prices.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
```

[Motley Fool page on the second trading day](https://www.fool.com/investing/2026/11/20/why-anthropic-stock-is-falling-today/) shows the day-two close with a 4:00 p.m. ET label. ## What this can and cannot show

The Fed's discussion and Anthropic's debut are separate evidence. The minutes document concerns about AI inflation pressure and losses if investment returns disappoint. Anthropic's first two trading days show a different, narrower fact: the stock began public trading above its IPO price, then fell while remaining above that IPO price at the end of day two.

**For markets:** A gain from the IPO price is not the same as a gain for someone who bought after trading began. The relevant starting price depends on when the shares were bought. These price comparisons also exclude fees and do not measure every investor's return.

**For the Fed:** October PCE, due `{python} stats['next_pce_date']`, is the next official reading of the price index used for its `{python} fmt(stats['fed_target'], 0)`% inflation goal. It can update the inflation picture before the meeting on `{python} stats['fomc_start_date']` to `{python} stats['fomc_end_date']`. It cannot explain this stock's first two trading days.

The timing does not establish that the minutes caused the share-price declines, that participants discussed this IPO, or that their conditional financing scenario occurred. Two trading days cannot separate changes in expected earnings from changes in required returns or other news. This post does not predict the next rate vote.

## Limitations

The minutes are a summary. "Almost all," "many," and "most" are the Federal Reserve's own counts, not a roll call a reader can recompute. The text does not name Anthropic.

The yield file ends on `{python} stats['dgs10_latest_date']` because that is the last observation in the `{python} stats['yield_release_date']` H.15 vintage. It has no observation for Anthropic's second trading day. The share prices are transcribed market reports, not an archived official price series. The original transcription has no retrieval timestamp, and another outlet's figure for the same trading day can differ.

CPI and PPI for October were released after the meeting. Reading the minutes as a comment on those prints misdates the discussion.

## Methodology & Data

The charts plot the cleaned yield column and the transcribed IPO and public-market prices. They do not recompute those prices. The stats step calculates each percentage change as ending price divided by starting price, minus one, expressed as a percentage. The inflation figures in the bridge come from the same locked vintages as the November 14 post and are not re-estimated here.

## References

**Federal Reserve documents.** The [October decision statement](https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20261028a.htm) records the target range and the vote. The [October minutes](https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomcminutes20261028.htm) record the staff assessment, the participants' discussion, and the market manager's account. The [minutes release notice](https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20261118a.htm) gives the publication date. The [September projections](https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomcprojtabl20260916.htm) are the source for the median funds rate only.

**Treasury-yield data.** [FRED DGS10](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DGS10) is the live constant-maturity series. This post plots the saved H.15 vintage of `{python} stats['yield_release_date']`, through `{python} stats['dgs10_latest_date']`. The live page can show later observations or revisions.

**Share-price reports.** The [Forbes report on the first trading day](https://www.forbes.com/sites/fionariley/2026/11/19/anthropic-ipo-live-stock-closes-day-at-97-up-more-than-17/) is the attribution saved for the IPO price, first public trade, and day-one close. The [Motley Fool page on the second trading day](https://www.fool.com/investing/2026/11/20/why-anthropic-stock-is-falling-today/) supplies the day-two close through its dated 4:00 p.m. quote label, not the earlier observation in the article text.

**Previous inflation analysis.** [October prices rose, but the annual CPI comparison is missing](https://gilboa.blog/posts/2026-11-14-october-cpi-ppi-missing-annual/) is the earlier post. This follow-up does not re-estimate those prints.
